meta.tagline: Stone streets in the castle's shadow, stories in the mist

pills: A castle on a volcanic rock

overview.title: Welcome to Edinburgh
overview.intro: Edinburgh is two cities, and each looks down at the other: the medieval Old Town pouring downhill from the castle on its volcanic rock, and the elegant, square-planned Georgian New Town. The extinct volcano of Arthur's Seat rises in the middle of it all, the sea mist called haar swallows the streets on some mornings, and a piper's drone echoes down the Royal Mile. This is the capital of storytellers — Stevenson, Conan Doyle, and the cafes where Harry Potter was born. And in August, the world's biggest arts festival turns the whole city into a stage.

local_word.definition: Scotland's best-loved word: gray, wet, misty, dispiriting weather — all in one syllable. When someone says 'it's a dreich day', the sky is lead-colored, but the Scot isn't sad about it: a dreich day is a pub day, a whisky day, a book day. Learn this word and you make peace with Scottish weather.

rules.title: Be ready for four seasons in one day
rules.description: Edinburgh's weather changes by the hour: sun at breakfast, rain at noon, wind by mid-afternoon. Dress in layers and pack a thin raincoat — umbrellas lose to the wind. When rain strikes, the nearest pub or bookshop is your shelter; Scots don't call that a ruined plan, they call it the plan.

rules.title: Book the castle and the big sights ahead
rules.description: Edinburgh Castle runs on timed tickets, and summer days end at a 'sold out' wall: buy online and early. Arthur's Seat, Calton Hill and the streets themselves are free — schedule the paid icons, improvise the free views.

rules.title: Come to August deliberately, or avoid it deliberately
rules.description: In August the Fringe triples the city: every cellar is a stage, every street a venue — rooms sell out months ahead and prices soar. If you want the festival spirit, plan early; if you want quiet Edinburgh, strike August from the calendar.

tip.label: The Edinburgh philosophy
tip.text: This city is understood on foot and uphill: every summit rewards with a view, every rain with a pub. Leave gaps in the plan — Edinburgh's best moments are found unplanned, inside the closes.

transport.title: Getting Around
transport.intro: The center is entirely walkable; the tram covers the airport and Lothian buses cover everything else — no car needed.

items.title: Arriving from the airport
items.description: The airport tram reaches Princes Street in 35 minutes: tickets from the machine or the app. The Airlink 100 bus runs through the night — a taxi costs three times the same road.

items.title: Two walkable towns
items.description: Everything between Old Town and New Town is within steps, but the steps are steep: the Royal Mile runs down a ridge and the side lanes are staircases. Comfortable shoes are non-negotiable — cobblestones don't negotiate with heels.

items.title: Lothian buses
items.description: The maroon buses reach every corner of the city: contactless payment caps at a daily maximum — the system does the ticket math for you. The top-deck front seat is the cheapest scenic tour in town.

items.title: The tram line
items.description: A single line runs from the airport to Leith: Princes Street and St Andrew Square are the key stops. The extension makes reaching the Leith waterfront easy — the practical line for a harbor outing.

items.title: Hill paths
items.description: The Arthur's Seat trails start at Holyrood: the summit is a 45-minute climb with route options for every level. Calton Hill is the ten-minute 'lazy view' — both are free.

callout.label: View tip
callout.text: On a windy but clear late afternoon, climb Calton Hill: castle, Old Town skyline and the Firth of Forth gather in one frame. Take your place twenty minutes before sunset — Edinburgh light is generous to photographers, and the wind is an enemy to hats.

stay.title: Where to Stay
stay.intro: The choice is between two towns: Old Town's stone atmosphere, New Town's Georgian elegance, or the village souls of Stockbridge and Leith.

local_word.definition: A narrow, tunneled passage branching off the Royal Mile: Edinburgh's hidden veins. Every close's name carries a story — a merchant's here, a ghost's there. Tourists walk the main street; those who know the city turn into the closes: beyond the stone arch wait courtyards, views and four centuries of whispers.

items.name: Old Town
items.description: Hotels in the stone buildings around the Royal Mile: the castle above, the closes at your door. You wake inside history — lively in summer and festival season, fairytale-quiet in winter.

items.name: New Town
items.description: Ordered squares, graceful facades and Princes Street shopping: five minutes to Old Town, one notch calmer. A balanced, stylish base — the best breakfast spots live here too.

items.name: Stockbridge
items.description: A village-like quarter by the water: a Sunday street market, independent shops, coffee roasters. A fifteen-minute walk to the center — for living Edinburgh like a local.

items.name: Leith
items.description: Waterfront restaurants, Michelin-starred kitchens and a transforming dock district: The Shore at dusk is one of the city's most pleasant corners. Linked to the center by tram — prices a notch kinder.

items.name: Bruntsfield and Morningside
items.description: Southern neighborhoods of cafes and bakeries beside the parks: a pleasant walk across the Meadows to the center. The balanced choice for families and quiet-night seekers.

best_time.title: When to Go
best_time.intro: Edinburgh's weather guarantees nothing, but its calendar is clear: August is festival madness, December is lights and Hogmanay, spring and autumn are the calm balance.

items.label: Spring
items.name: Waking Gardens
items.subtitle: Spring · Blossoming Meadows, stretching days
items.description: The Meadows drown in cherry blossom, the days lengthen fast, and the festival crowds are still far away. The year's most balanced window for Arthur's Seat trails and close-hunting — the weather still springs surprises, so layer up.

callout.label: May tip
callout.text: Climb Arthur's Seat early on a May morning: the wind is sharp at the summit but the view is crystal — castle, firth and city at your feet. Descend in time for the Stockbridge market and breakfast is your reward.

items.label: Summer
items.name: Festival Madness
items.subtitle: Summer · Fringe stages, full streets, long light
items.description: In August the Fringe, the International Festival and the Military Tattoo share the stage: the city becomes one vast performance and the queues run past midnight. Light lasts until ten — the energy is unmatched, and so are the prices and crowds.

callout.label: August note
callout.text: Never arrive in festival August without a plan: book your room months ahead, pre-book shows, but leave one or two daily gaps — the Fringe's soul is walking into an unknown show whose flyer you liked, at the last minute.

items.label: Autumn
items.name: Season of Golden Mist
items.subtitle: Autumn · Orange parks, dreich days, pub fires
items.description: The city shakes off festival fatigue, the parks turn gold, and the haar swallows the castle each morning and gives it back. Pub fires are lit and whisky season opens — these are the months when Edinburgh is most itself.

callout.label: October tip
callout.text: Walk Victoria Street as its lights come on in October, then order a dram by a pub fire: the dreich outside, you inside — that is the exact formula of a Scottish autumn. The Samhuinn fire festival, Halloween's ancestor, falls this month too.

items.label: Winter
items.name: Lights and Hogmanay
items.subtitle: Winter · Christmas markets, New Year festival, short days
items.description: In December the Christmas market floods Princes Street Gardens with light; at New Year, Hogmanay becomes a three-day city festival — torchlight procession, concerts and midnight fireworks. The days are short, the atmosphere dense.

callout.label: Hogmanay tip
callout.text: If you're seeing in the New Year in Edinburgh, buy Hogmanay tickets early: the street party is capacity-limited. On January 1st, join the 'Loony Dook' plunge into the freezing sea if you dare — or applaud from the shore; either way you've started the year the Scottish way.

eat.title: What to Eat
eat.intro: Scottish cooking looks modest and lands solid: the spice of haggis, the freshness of salmon, the smoke of whisky — all at pub warmth.

local_word.definition: A measure of whisky: the base unit of Scottish table culture. 'A wee dram' is the shared language of invitation, celebration and consolation. Adding a drop of water is not a faux pas but the craft that opens the aroma — ask the bartender for a water dropper and drink your dram at your own setting.

items.name: Haggis, neeps and tatties
items.description: Scotland's national dish: spiced haggis with mashed turnip and potato. It sounds like a dare and tastes deep and peppery — asking for whisky sauce on top is a legitimate modern touch.
items.tag: National classic · try the whisky sauce

items.name: The whisky dram ritual
items.description: From Islay's smoke to Speyside's honey: a good whisky bar draws you a map by asking questions. A tasting flight starts at three drams — have your answer ready for 'peaty or sweet?'
items.tag: By the flight · ask the bartender

items.name: Fish and chips with chippy sauce
items.description: Crisp-battered cod and thick-cut chips: the Edinburgh difference is the brown 'chippy sauce' — the local blend of vinegar and brown sauce. When asked 'salt and sauce?', say 'aye' and follow the city's custom.

items.name: Cullen skink
items.description: A cream soup of smoked haddock and potato: the northeast coast's gift to Edinburgh tables. The most honest answer to a dreich noon — with fresh bread and plenty of butter.

items.name: The full Scottish breakfast
items.description: Sausage, eggs, beans and the star players: square (lorne) sausage, tattie scone and a slice of haggis. It holds you till noon — queueing for breakfast is a Stockbridge tradition.
items.tag: A challenge to the day · with tattie scone

items.name: Cranachan and shortbread
items.description: Cranachan — raspberries with cream, honey, whisky and toasted oats — and buttery shortbread beside it: two classics of the Scottish sweet course. Closing with a cheese board and a dram instead of dessert is equally native.

callout.label: Table rule
callout.text: In Edinburgh the lunch menus run at half the evening price: schedule the big meal for noon. Against the Royal Mile tourist traps, turn one street aside — the Leith waterfront and Stockbridge are the most honest addresses for the price-to-flavor balance.

hidden_gems.title: Hidden Corners
hidden_gems.intro: Everyone sees the castle; these six are Edinburgh's misty, storied hidden pages.

items.name: Dean Village
items.description: A medieval milling village ten minutes from the center: stone houses, the sound of the Water of Leith and ivy-covered facades. Go early in the morning — from the bridge, it's hard to believe you're still in a city.

items.name: Circus Lane
items.description: A cobbled old mews lane behind Stockbridge, lined with flowers: with its church tower backdrop and begonia pots, the city's most graceful frame. A five-minute lane means a half-hour photo stop.

items.rarity: A village pub by a loch
items.name: Duddingston and the Sheep Heid Inn
items.description: A village hidden behind Arthur's Seat: its loch, its kirk, and a pub serving since 1360. Descend from the summit this way — a dram at the inn with its old skittle alley is the walk's earned reward.

items.name: The Water of Leith walkway
items.description: The stream path that secretly crosses the city: from Dean Village to Stockbridge and on to the Botanic Garden, walking to the sound of water. The city's noise stays one level above — Edinburgh's hidden green corridor.

items.name: Calton Hill
items.description: A ten-minute climb to the hill of monuments: the unfinished 'Parthenon', the observatory and the city's most famous panorama. Everyone comes at sunset, but the hill is wide — find your own stone and watch the light descend.

items.name: The Old Town's independent bookshops
items.description: The second-hand bookshops around Grassmarket and Victoria Street: maps, old editions and Scottish poetry between the shelves. The best shelter when rain strikes — the rule that 'a dreich day is a bookshop day' is proven here.

callout.label: Mist strategy
callout.text: Edinburgh's hidden corners pair with the weather: Calton Hill and Duddingston on clear days, bookshops and museums on dreich days, Dean Village on any day. Don't resent the sky — in this city every kind of weather has its own route.

traps.title: Tourist Traps
traps.intro: Edinburgh is an honest city; its traps are small but classic — know these four and save the budget for a dram.

items.name: Mass-produced 'Scottish' cashmere and tartan
items.description: In some Royal Mile windows, imported goods labeled 'Scottish cashmere' sell at hand-loom prices; the bagpipe loudspeaker doesn't change the label of origin.
items.instead: Read the label: look for 'Made in Scotland' and choose the mill brands. For real tartan, go to an established shop that asks about clan patterns and sells by the meter — a merchant who tells the story knows the cloth.

items.name: The ticket queue at the castle gate
items.description: Edinburgh Castle runs timed entry: arrive at the gate on a summer day and you meet either a long queue or the 'sold out' sign.
items.instead: Buy a timed ticket from the official site days ahead; the first morning slot is best for calm and for views. To hear the One O'Clock Gun, be on the ramparts at 13:00.

items.name: Arriving in August at the last minute
items.description: In festival month, room prices triple or quadruple and still sell out; late seekers get flung to the city's edge or over budget.
items.instead: Lock the festival plan months ahead, or shift your visit to September: the same city at half the price with room to breathe. Early September's post-festival calm is Edinburgh's secret golden fortnight.

items.name: Mediocre ghost tours
items.description: Some graveyard and underground tours fill tickets with costumed jump-scares; the history is thin and the experience stays at funfair level.
items.instead: Read reviews and pick small-group tours known for storytelling; alternatively, documented underground tours like the Real Mary King's Close frighten with history — a real shiver instead of a cheap jump-scare.

callout.label: Golden rule
callout.text: In Edinburgh the most expensive things are tickets and August; the most precious things are free: the hills, the closes, the street music and the views. Save the money for one good dram, one good table and pre-booked tickets — collect the rest on foot.

itinerary.title: Ready-Made Itineraries
itinerary.intro: If you hate planning, follow these flows. Times are flexible; keep the spirit, break the order.

plans.title: If You Have 1 Day
plans.subtitle: From castle to Calton Hill — a day of stories

steps.title: Full Scottish breakfast
steps.description: Take on the day with tattie scone and a slice of haggis: there are many slopes today, and fuel is essential.

steps.title: Edinburgh Castle
steps.description: Enter on the first timed slot: the crown room, the war memorial and the city from the ramparts. Be out before the One O'Clock Gun.

steps.title: The Royal Mile by its closes
steps.description: Walk the passages, not the main street: courtyards, views and St Giles' Cathedral. Pause among the colored facades of Victoria Street.

steps.title: Lunch and a museum
steps.description: Cullen skink or haggis around Grassmarket; then the roof terrace of the National Museum — free, with a view.

steps.title: Arthur's Seat or Calton Hill
steps.description: Choose by your energy: the 45-minute summit climb or the 10-minute hill of monuments. Both are generous at sunset.

steps.title: Pub evening and a dram
steps.description: Dinner by a pub fire, then a whisky flight: find your answer to 'peaty or sweet?' If there's live folk music, the night stretches on its own.

plans.title: If You Have 3 Days
plans.subtitle: Two towns, hills and a harbor — the full Edinburgh

steps.title: Classic Edinburgh
steps.description: The 1-day flow above: breakfast, the castle, the closes, a museum, a summit view, a pub and a dram.

steps.title: New Town and village corners
steps.description: Morning among the Georgian facades and Princes Street Gardens; coffee and shop-browsing in Stockbridge (street market if it's Sunday); afternoon at Dean Village + the Water of Leith walk to the Botanic Garden; evening photo at Circus Lane and a neighborhood bistro.

steps.title: Summit and harbor
steps.description: Morning on Arthur's Seat, descending via Duddingston for lunch at the Sheep Heid Inn; tram to Leith in the afternoon — a waterfront walk and the Royal Yacht Britannia; farewell seafood dinner on The Shore + one last dram.

phrases.title: 5-Word Survival Kit
phrases.intro: Scottish English comes with its own dictionary; these five phrases melt the ice instantly in pub and street.

items.meaning: Yes — short, clear and Scottish; you'll hear it a hundred times a day
Small, a little — 'a wee dram', 'a wee walk'; the endearing word that fits any sentence
Beautiful, lovely — said of views and people alike; the 'bonnie Scotland' cliché is earned
Cheers! — Gaelic for 'good health'; said as the dram rises, and respected at the bar
How's it going? — the Scottish 'what's up'; the answer is usually 'no bad'

checklist.completion_message: Slàinte mhath! You've lived the city of mist and stories the way it deserves!
